triage.name: Gallstones
triage.reason: Very common biliary colic presentation with classic postprandial right upper quadrant pain, exam, labs and ultrasound leading to diagnosis.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'right upper quadrant ultrasound' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']
presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common in women than men, especially before age 60
Higher prevalence in Native American and Mexican American populations
Prevalence increases with age in both sexes
Often discovered incidentally on imaging done for other reasons

risk_factors.text: Native American or Mexican American ancestry

comorbidities: Crohn disease or prior ileal resection
Hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis)
social_history: Diets high in fat and refined carbohydrates

chief_complaints.text: My stomach hurts under my right ribs
The pain comes in waves after I eat
I feel sick to my stomach

hpi.onset: Sudden, often awakening the patient from sleep or starting within an hour after a meal
hpi.duration: Episodes last 30 minutes to several hours; symptoms may have been recurring for weeks to months
hpi.progression: Steady intense pain that plateaus rather than building continuously; resolves spontaneously or with pain medication, but recurs with subsequent fatty meals
hpi.radiation: May radiate to the right shoulder, right scapula, or mid-back
hpi.quality: Constant, aching, or pressure-like; sometimes described as gripping
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe, often 6–9/10 at peak
hpi.timing: Postprandial, typically 30–60 minutes after eating, especially after fatty or fried foods; may occur at night
relieving: Nothing consistently; sometimes sitting upright or walking helps slightly
Pain medication may partially relieve it

associated_symptoms.text: Dark urine or light-colored stools (if bile duct obstruction)

pertinent_negatives: Pain that starts in the epigastrium and migrates to the right lower quadrant
Pain that is clearly pleuritic or positional
Burning epigastric pain relieved by food or antacids
Pain radiating to the left arm or jaw
Weight loss or loss of appetite

argues_against: Pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant
Pain relieved by bowel movement or antacids
Pain radiating to the left arm or jaw
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with vague abdominal discomfort, anorexia, or confusion rather than classic colicky pain; pain may be less severe.
missing_classic_features: Severe postprandial right upper quadrant pain

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to normal pregnancy discomfort; right upper quadrant pain can be mistaken for preeclampsia or HELLP syndrome.
May have atypical or blunted pain due to autonomic neuropathy; higher risk of severe complications like emphysematous cholecystitis.
Symptoms may be similar but physical exam is more difficult; higher risk of complications and technical difficulty with surgery.
Gallstones are uncommon in children; when present, they are often associated with hemolytic disease or obesity and may present with vague abdominal pain.

general.mild: Comfortable between episodes; mild distress only during an attack
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, prefers to lie still, may be nauseated
general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, guarding the right upper quadrant
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, may be confused or hypotensive

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and epigastrium
Hook the fingers under the right costal margin and ask the patient to take a deep breath
findings.finding: Inspiratory arrest or marked pain on deep palpation of the right upper quadrant (Murphy sign)

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough, or gently release deep pressure
findings.finding: Pain with jarring, suggesting peritoneal irritation

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and right costal margin
Inspect the sclera and skin in natural light
Measure temperature and assess for rigors
Auscultate bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Pelvic exam when a gynecologic cause is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness or adnexal mass

labs.caveat: Normal in uncomplicated biliary colic; a rising white count with fever suggests acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, or another complication.
Normal in simple cholelithiasis; elevation suggests a stone in the common bile duct or another cause of obstruction.
A direct (conjugated) predominance points to obstruction of the bile duct rather than hemolysis.
Rises with bile duct obstruction; a cholestatic pattern with a high alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin suggests a common bile duct stone.
Confirms that an elevated alkaline phosphatase is hepatobiliary in origin.
Transaminases are usually normal or only mildly elevated unless a stone is passing through the common bile duct.
Order when pain is epigastric or radiates to the back; a stone impacted at the ampulla can cause gallstone pancreatitis.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and surgery; rules out ectopic pregnancy.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line study for suspected gallstones in all patients

findings.text: Echogenic foci within the gallbladder with posterior acoustic shadowing (gallstones)
Sonographic Murphy sign (focal tenderness over the gallbladder with the probe)
Dilated common bile duct over 6 mm (suggests a common bile duct stone)
Sludge or biliary microlithiasis without discrete stones
Gallbladder not visualized or obscured by bowel gas (nondiagnostic study)

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected common bile duct stone when ultrasound is nondiagnostic and before ERCP

findings.text: Filling defect within the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis)
Dilated intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts

imaging.preferred_when: High likelihood of a common bile duct stone, especially with cholangitis or worsening obstruction

findings.text: Stone or filling defect in the common bile duct, with or without ductal dilation
Bile duct stones can be removed at the same procedure (sphincterotomy and extraction)

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When another cause of abdominal pain is suspected or complications are being assessed

findings.text: Gallstones may be seen, but many are isodense and missed on CT
Gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, or fat stranding (cholecystitis)
Pancreatic enlargement or peripancreatic fluid (gallstone pancreatitis)
Usually normal; only about 10–15% of gallstones are calcified enough to be seen

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected acute cholecystitis when ultrasound is equivocal

findings.text: Nonvisualization of the gallbladder with tracer uptake in the liver and bile ducts (cystic duct obstruction)

initial.why: Looks for leukocytosis suggesting cholecystitis or another complication
Assesses bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases for bile duct obstruction
Rules out gallstone pancreatitis when pain is epigastric or radiates to the back
Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before imaging and any intervention
First-line test to confirm gallstones and assess the gallbladder wall and bile ducts

supporting.why: Detects common bile duct stones noninvasively
supporting.only_if: suspected common bile duct stone with a dilated duct or abnormal liver tests

supporting.why: Both diagnoses and treats common bile duct stones
supporting.only_if: high likelihood of a common bile duct stone, cholangitis, or worsening obstruction
suspected acute cholecystitis with an equivocal ultrasound

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for uncomplicated gallstones; misses many stones and adds radiation
not_indicated.only_if: another cause of abdominal pain is suspected or complications are being assessed

not_indicated.why: Rarely shows gallstones and does not change management
No role in right upper quadrant pain
Not routinely needed unless a urinary cause is suspected
Not needed unless cardiac pain is suspected
Not part of the acute evaluation of gallstones

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging or surgery in anyone who could be pregnant
Ultrasound first; if it shows gallstones without duct dilation or abnormal liver tests, no further imaging is needed
Dilated common bile duct or abnormal liver tests raise concern for a common bile duct stone and prompt MRCP or ERCP
Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain suggest cholangitis and need urgent biliary drainage
Peritonitis or hemodynamic instability goes to surgery without waiting for further imaging

differential.name: Acute cholecystitis
differential.why_considered: Gallstones are the cause of most acute cholecystitis; the pain is in the same location and follows the same postprandial pattern.
differential.trigger: Pain lasting more than 6 hours with fever, leukocytosis, or a positive Murphy sign

history: Pain is constant and lasts more than 6 hours rather than resolving between episodes
Fever and chills
Pain is not relieved by medication or position change
exam: Marked right upper quadrant tenderness with inspiratory arrest (Murphy sign)
Guarding or a palpable tender gallbladder
labs: Mild bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase elevation
imaging: Nonvisualization of the gallbladder on HIDA scan

differential.name: Choledocholithiasis with cholangitis
differential.why_considered: A stone that migrates into the common bile duct causes the same right upper quadrant pain and can obstruct bile flow.
differential.trigger: Fever with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot triad), or hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad)

history: Jaundice with dark urine and light-colored stools
Fever with rigors
Pruritus
exam: Hypotension or altered mental status in severe cases
labs: Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT
imaging: Dilated common bile duct over 6 mm on ultrasound
Filling defect in the common bile duct on MRCP
Stone seen and removable at ERCP

differential.name: Gallstone pancreatitis
differential.why_considered: A stone impacted at the ampulla can trigger pancreatitis, which shares epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.
differential.trigger: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting and a lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal

history: Pain radiates to the back and is relieved by leaning forward
Persistent vomiting
Pain is more epigastric than right upper quadrant
labs: Lipase elevated more than three times the upper limit of normal
imaging: Pancreatic enlargement and peripancreatic fluid on CT
Dilated common bile duct suggesting an impacted stone

differential.name: Peptic ulcer disease
differential.why_considered: Epigastric pain is a common complaint that overlaps with biliary colic.

history: Burning epigastric pain relieved by food or antacids
Nocturnal pain
NSAID use or Helicobacter pylori history
exam: Epigastric tenderness without right upper quadrant localization
labs: Positive H. pylori stool antigen or breath test

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Postprandial epigastric burning and nausea can mimic biliary colic.

history: Heartburn and regurgitation after meals
Symptoms worse when lying flat
Relief with antacids or proton pump inhibitors
exam: Epigastric tenderness without right upper quadrant findings

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Inferior myocardial infarction can present with epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.
differential.trigger: Epigastric pain with diaphoresis, dyspnea, or cardiac risk factors

history: Chest pressure or pain radiating to the left arm or jaw
Exertional onset or dyspnea
Cardiac risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, or smoking
ecg: ST elevation or depression in inferior leads

differential.name: Right lower lobe pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Pleuritic right-sided pain can be referred to the right upper quadrant and epigastrium.

history: Cough, fever, and sputum production
Pleuritic pain worse with deep breathing
exam: Crackles or decreased breath sounds at the right base
imaging: Right lower lobe infiltrate on chest x-ray or CT

differential.name: Kidney stone
differential.why_considered: Right-sided flank and abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting can be confused with biliary colic.

history: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Patient writhes and cannot get comfortable
Dysuria or hematuria

severity.mild: Biliary colic: episodes of right upper quadrant pain lasting 30 minutes to several hours, resolving spontaneously, with no fever, normal white count, and normal liver tests
severity.moderate: Acute cholecystitis: constant pain over 6 hours, fever, leukocytosis, and gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid on ultrasound
severity.severe: Cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis: jaundice, fever, hypotension, or a lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal, requiring urgent drainage or intensive care
severity.critical: Septic shock from cholangitis or severe necrotizing pancreatitis with organ failure

red_flags.finding: Fever with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain

red_flags.meaning: Septic shock from cholangitis or severe pancreatitis

red_flags.finding: Lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal
Persistent pain over 6 hours with fever and leukocytosis
red_flags.meaning: Acute cholecystitis rather than simple biliary colic

complications.name: Choledocholithiasis
clues: Dilated common bile duct on ultrasound

complications.name: Gallstone pancreatitis
clues: Epigastric pain radiating to the back
Lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal

complications.name: Gallstone ileus
clues: Bowel obstruction in an older adult

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, sometimes radiating to the right shoulder, right scapula, or mid-back

key_questions.question: When did the pain start, and how long does an episode last?
key_questions.looking_for: Episodes lasting 30 minutes to several hours that resolve; pain lasting more than 6 hours suggests cholecystitis

key_questions.question: What were you doing when the pain started? Does it come on after eating?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset 30–60 minutes after a meal, especially a fatty or fried meal, or waking the patient at night

key_questions.question: Does the pain come in waves, or is it constant?
key_questions.looking_for: Steady, intense pain that plateaus rather than building continuously; recurring episodes over weeks to months

key_questions.question: Does anything make the pain better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with fatty meals, large meals, lying flat, or bending over; nothing consistently relieves it

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea or vomiting with the pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea and vomiting accompanying the pain

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and chills suggest acute cholecystitis or cholangitis rather than simple biliary colic

key_questions.question: Have you noticed yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pale stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Jaundice, dark urine, or light-colored stools suggest a common bile duct stone or obstruction

key_questions.question: Have you had any itching?
key_questions.looking_for: Pruritus from cholestasis when the bile duct is obstructed

key_questions.question: Have you had gallstones or gallbladder problems before, or any abdominal surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior episodes of biliary colic, prior cholecystitis, or prior cholecystectomy

key_questions.question: Do you take any estrogen-containing medications, such as birth control pills or hormone replacement therapy?
Has anyone in your family had gallstones or gallbladder surgery?
Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy increases gallstone risk and must be excluded before imaging and any intervention

key_questions.question: What is your typical diet and activity level? Have you lost weight recently?
key_questions.looking_for: High-fat diet, sedentary lifestyle, or rapid weight loss

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, blood in the urine, or flank pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a urinary cause such as a kidney stone

key_questions.question: Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or pain radiating to the left arm or jaw?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present raises concern for acute coronary syndrome

reasoning_points: Recurrent episodes of right upper quadrant or epigastric pain lasting 30 minutes to several hours, coming on 30–60 minutes after fatty meals
Pain may radiate to the right shoulder, right scapula, or mid-back
Nausea and vomiting accompany the pain
Risk factors such as female sex, age over 40, obesity, pregnancy, estrogen use, and family history
Right upper quadrant tenderness on exam without fever or jaundice in uncomplicated disease
Normal or only mildly abnormal white count, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lipase in simple biliary colic
Right upper quadrant ultrasound showing echogenic foci in the gallbladder with posterior acoustic shadowing
Pregnancy excluded before imaging and any intervention
Red flags such as fever, jaundice, or pain lasting more than 6 hours prompt evaluation for cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis

easy: Middle-aged woman with obesity and classic postprandial right upper quadrant pain
Pain radiating to the right shoulder after a fatty meal
Right upper quadrant tenderness on exam
Ultrasound showing gallstones with acoustic shadowing
medium: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with a mildly elevated lipase, raising concern for gallstone pancreatitis
Older adult with vague abdominal discomfort and anorexia rather than classic colicky pain
Patient with a dilated common bile duct or abnormal liver tests suggesting a common bile duct stone
Pregnant patient with right upper quadrant pain that could be mistaken for preeclampsia or HELLP syndrome
hard: Patient with diabetes and blunted pain from autonomic neuropathy presenting with atypical symptoms
Gallstones found incidentally on imaging done for another reason, with no biliary symptoms
Older adult with bowel obstruction from gallstone ileus and pneumobilia on imaging
Patient with right lower lobe pneumonia or acute coronary syndrome presenting with epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
